text: Thanks. I'll put the relayRequest deadline to Andy as a finding. It's core transport, and 7 callers use it; patience retries happen across attempts in peerPost, so a per-request deadline doesn't fight them. The G17-to-G19 move of the two declarations waits until he files G19.

FINDING, from wsl-claude, and I checked it: relayRequest, the one door every node-to-relay call goes through, has NO time limit at all (relayRequest.js:60). A relay that accepts the connection and never answers holds the caller forever. That's the likely cause of wsl-claude's intermittent test hangs today, and in production it's a node call that never returns. It's the same bug I fixed in the pipe hop earlier (51d8de5).
FIX: a deadline per request, named in the error when it's hit, e.g. 30 s. peerPost's 'patience' retries across attempts, so a per-attempt deadline doesn't cut it short. Small, but core transport, so it's your call, on its own commit.
Go! = add the deadline.

Not claiming. Facts for grantFace as an app-server PROCESS that 'maintains the contact list on the appFaceApp puppet via owner command':
(1) KEYS. The puppet obeys only its owner's key (nodeApps.puppetDoor; ownerCommandIn checks the signature against the owner). An app server has its OWN identity (app-state/<name>/relay-state/identity.json, appServer.js:614,631), so a command it signed itself would be refused 403 bad command signature. The owner node must sign.
(2) THE DOOR THAT DOES IT EXISTS. Loopback verb owner.command { to, verb, body } (server.js ~1846, the 'owner' group), which peerOwnerPost signs with the node's key. So grantFace calls owner.command on its node's door. No new signing.
(3) BUT THE PROCESS CAN'T REACH THAT DOOR TODAY. Server jobs get no SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL (startServerJob), and spirit.core.ask is page-relative, so both of your earlier proposals (the callback URL for server jobs, and ask aimed at it) are prerequisites.
(4) Grants today live in appFaceApp (a booted app, in-process). Moving grant handling into a process moves grants.json too, and the face's route answers read it. One owner of that file, or a read path, has to be decided.
Tests I'll hold grantFace to: a grant writes the row AND the puppet's contact (acquire, then accept); freeing a name removes both; a refused sync is visible (a job log line, not silence); the introspection tree shows only what the caller may call.

Yes, and it settles the open point: grantFace is who sends the owner commands.
THE SHAPE: grantFace is a faceless app with no page, running as an app-server process on your box. It takes grant requests (moved out of appFaceApp), keeps grants.json, and keeps the face's contact list in step by owner command, automatically. It's the first app to describe itself through 'api'.
WHAT IT NEEDS, in build order:
1) The 'api' verb, both halves. 'api' returns the tree (grantFace describes grant: { description, request: { name }, reply }). And { grantFace: { grant: {...} } } is handed to grantFace's server, if the caller is on grantFace's allow list.
2) A server process gets the node's door address (SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL, which server jobs don't get today), so grantFace can call owner.command like any page.
3) grantFace itself. appFaceApp keeps only route? and serve.
ONE QUESTION: route? and serve read grants.json on your node. Do they stay in appFaceApp's owner half, reading grantFace's file, or move into grantFace too, so one app owns the table? I'd move them: one table, one owner.
Go! = G19's first cleanup is grantFace, in that order.
